subject: chemistry
title: NMR spectroscopy
key_idea: NMR gives one peak per environment of ¹³C or ¹H atoms. Chemical shift shows the type of environment, peak area the number of protons, and splitting the neighbours.

blocks.text: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy tells you about the carbon and hydrogen atoms in a molecule. This section covers the ideas shared by carbon-13 and proton NMR.

items.meaning: The set of atoms of one element in the same position in the molecule, with the same surroundings. Atoms in the same environment give one peak.
The position of a peak on the scale, in parts per million (ppm), measured from the TMS peak.
Tetramethylsilane, (CH₃)₄Si, the standard that sets δ = 0.

items: Nuclei with an odd mass number, such as ¹H and ¹³C, behave like tiny magnets.
In a strong magnetic field, they absorb radio waves of a particular frequency.
The frequency depends on the **environment** of the nucleus, as the nearby atoms shield it. This is the chemical shift.
Atoms bonded to electronegative atoms or to C=O have a larger shift.
Each peak is one environment. More electronegative neighbours give a larger δ.
Symmetry in a molecule reduces the number of peaks.

blocks.text: Carbon-13 NMR shows the carbon atoms in a molecule. The spectra are simple because each environment gives a single peak.

items: The number of peaks equals the number of **different carbon environments**.
Each peak's position shows the type of carbon.
In ¹³C spectra the peaks are single lines (the spectra are proton decoupled), and they give no splitting information.
Spectra are simpler than ¹H spectra, since there are fewer peaks.

blocks.text: Propan-2-ol has three carbon atoms but only two peaks. The two CH₃ carbons are in identical environments, so they share one peak. Propan-1-ol has three carbon environments and so three peaks.

items: Count the peaks to find the number of carbon environments.
Use δ to say what type each carbon is.

blocks.text: Proton (¹H) NMR gives three pieces of evidence for each environment: its shift, its area and its splitting.

items: The area under each peak is proportional to the number of protons in that environment.
The relative areas, from an integration trace or ratio numbers, give the simplest ratio of protons.
A ratio of 3 : 2 : 1 means three, two and one proton in the three environments, or a multiple of this.
A proton with **n** equivalent protons on the neighbouring carbon atoms splits into **n + 1** lines.
Protons on the same carbon do not split each other.
Singlet: no neighbouring protons. Doublet (1 : 1): one. Triplet (1 : 2 : 1): two. Quartet (1 : 3 : 3 : 1): three.

diagram.alt: Pick a molecule to see its number of carbon peaks, proton environments, area ratio and splitting.

items: Shift tells the environment, area the number of protons, splitting the neighbours.
Use n + 1 on the adjacent carbons, not on the same carbon.

blocks.text: A spectrum needs a reference point and a solvent that does not give its own peaks. This section covers both, and a trick for O–H and N–H protons.

items: **TMS** is added as the reference. Its peak is set at δ = 0 and all other shifts are measured from it.
The sample is dissolved in a **deuterated solvent** such as CDCl₃. Deuterium (²H) does not absorb in the proton NMR range, so the solvent gives no peaks to hide the sample's.
Add a drop of **D₂O** and shake. The O–H or N–H protons swap for deuterium, and their peaks vanish from the spectrum.

blocks.text: Comparing a spectrum before and after adding D₂O shows which peak is the O–H or N–H proton.

items: TMS is the zero point of the δ scale.
Deuterated solvents give no ¹H peaks, and D₂O removes O–H and N–H peaks.

checks.q: State the number of peaks in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of propanone and in its ¹H NMR spectrum.
checks.a: Two peaks in ¹³C (the two CH₃ carbons are equivalent, plus C=O). One peak in ¹H (all six protons are equivalent).

checks.q: A ¹H NMR spectrum has a triplet at δ 1.0 and a quartet at δ 2.4, in the ratio 3 : 2. Explain the splitting.
checks.a: The CH₃ protons have two neighbouring protons (CH₂), so n + 1 = 3, a triplet. The CH₂ protons have three neighbouring protons (CH₃), so n + 1 = 4, a quartet.

checks.q: Describe how D₂O is used to identify an O–H proton.
checks.a: Run the spectrum, add D₂O and shake, then run it again. The peak from the O–H proton disappears because the H is exchanged for D.

blocks.text: You must be able to recognise aromatic protons from their shift, but you are not asked to analyse their splitting.

items: Aromatic protons appear in the range δ 6.0–9.0.
You may also be asked to predict the ¹³C or ¹H spectrum of a molecule you are given: count the environments, estimate each δ from the data sheet and give the splitting.
Chemical shift values are provided on the data sheet.

blocks.text: ¹H spectra can be recorded in CCl₄ as well as in deuterated solvents, as CCl₄ has no hydrogen atoms.

items: TMS is suitable as a standard because it gives **one sharp peak**, since all 12 protons are equivalent.
It is **inert**, so it does not react with the sample.
It is **volatile**, so it is easy to remove afterwards.
Its peak lies at a lower shift than almost every other peak, so it does not overlap.
Splitting patterns are limited to doublet, triplet and quartet in aliphatic compounds.

blocks.text: Splitting patterns are limited to singlet, doublet, triplet, quartet and multiplet.

items: A pattern of more than four lines is called a multiplet.
You may be asked to predict the shift and splitting for each proton in a molecule you are given, and then to use them to suggest a structure.
